concepts.title: Ain-i-Akbari as an Administrative Record
concepts.definition: The Ain-i-Akbari, compiled by Abu'l Fazl in 1595 within the Akbar Nama, recorded the empire's provinces, revenue schedules, castes, officials and regulations; historians value its data while cautioning that it recorded ideals and court perspectives more than village realities.
concepts.key_idea: The Ain is a window with a frame: its statistics are precious, but they report the state's eye view of the sixteenth century.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehs204.txt Ain-i-Akbari content and its limitations sections

solution_steps.explain: the Ain was completed in 1595 under Abu'l Fazl
revenue schedules, provincial statistics and court regulations fill its books
its numbers reflect administrative ideals, not always village practice

concepts.title: Land Revenue: Measurement and Zabt
concepts.definition: Mughal land revenue rested on measurement of fields, assessment of crops by cash prices, and the zabt system in provinces like the subas of the core; officials used the dahsala schedule, recognised jins-i-kamil (perfect crops) as assessment standards, and revenue officials recorded every pargana.
concepts.key_idea: Zabt fixed cash demands on measured fields, shifting risk onto peasants while standardising the state's largest income source.

solution_steps.explain: _state figures in bigha fed the assessment schedules

concepts.title: Village Society: Panchayats and Women
concepts.definition: Village panchayats of elders levied taxes, settled disputes and regulated conduct, with the muqaddam and patwari as office-holders; women worked in fields, spinning and artisanal trades, and petitions to panchayats show both their agency and the limits set by household hierarchy.
concepts.key_idea: The panchayat was part court, part welfare body: it taxed marriages and disputes, and sometimes pleaded with the state for peasants.

solution_steps.explain: elders enforced norms, levied seigneurial dues and arbitrated
muqaddams headed villages while patwaris kept records
petitions show women claiming wages and dignity within limits

concepts.title: Zamindars, Jagirs and Peasant Resistance
concepts.definition: Zamindars held hereditary rights over land and castles, commanded armed followers, and mediated between state and peasantry; the state assigned revenue rights as jagirs to mansabdars, and tensions among raiyats, zamindars and jagirdars produced frequent rural conflicts and rebellions.
concepts.key_idea: Three-tiered pressure - state demand, zamindar power, peasant survival - made the Mughal countryside a negotiated, often contested, order.

solution_steps.explain: hereditary claim, armed retainers and fortress made zamindars local powers

flight, refusal and revolt answered excessive demands

solution_template.explain: panchayats settled disputes within the village
they collected taxes for community needs like weddings
they petitioned officials on behalf of peasants

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain why zamindars were powerful intermediaries in the Mughal countryside.

solution_template.explain: zamindari passed through families and commanded local legitimacy
forts and followers made coercion of zamindars costly
the state had to negotiate revenue through them, sharing power
